description: **Presence is now declared, never inferred.** Every flag and every positional argument must declare exactly one of `presence="required"`, `presence="optional"` or `default=<value>`; declaring none or two is a registration-time error. `default=None` is refused with a redirect to `presence="optional"`, the arg `required=` field is deleted, a repeatable or dict flag no longer defaults silently to `[]` / `{}`, and a mutex member declares its own optionality instead of receiving an exemption.

**`ctx.provided(name)`, and presence published everywhere it is asked about.** `ctx.provided` answers whether the invocation caused a flag's value -- true for `cli`, `env`, `config` and `implied`, false for `default` and `infra` -- so no handler reconstructs that boolean out of `ctx.source`. `--dump-schema` emits a `presence` key on every flag and arg entry, plus a `default` exactly when presence is `"default"` (empty collections included); help renders exactly one marker per line (`[required]`, `[optional]` or `[default: <value>]`), with required positionals and declared empty collections now visible; and MCP tool schemas read requiredness straight off the declaration.

**A positional argument's bool default renders lowercase in help.** A positional now shows `[default: true]` / `[default: false]` exactly as a flag does; it rendered `[default: True]` through Python's own `str`, so a single help page could show both spellings of the same value. Every other value type -- strings, numbers, collections -- already rendered identically on both surfaces and is now pinned that way.

**Fixed positional arg order with stacked `@strictcli.arg` decorators.** Two or more stacked `@strictcli.arg` decorators bound argv bottom-up, so the arguments were assigned in reverse declaration order (and listed reversed in help). They now bind top-down, matching the `args=[...]` list form.

**README explains the Python-shaped declaration surface.** The package README now states that the Python implementation is not a port of the Go or TypeScript ones: the surface is Python's own (decorators, keyword arguments, the `Flag` dataclass, `ValueError` at registration), some enforcement exists only in Python, and what the three implementations hold identical is behavior rather than spelling.

**Choice flags: a choice is a declaration scope.** A choice flag elects exactly one of its declared choices, and each choice owns the flags that exist only while it is elected. `@strictcli.choice` declares a choice as a frozen dataclass whose fields (declared with `strictcli.sub_flag` / `sub_choice_flag`) are the scope's flags; `@strictcli.choice_flag` attaches the selector, with `elect_by="selector-token"` (`--via email`) or `elect_by="member-flags"` (`--profile work` / `--all-profiles`, payload declared with `strictcli.member_value`). The elected value reaches the handler as one tagged record consumed by `match`, parsing stays order-independent, and choice flags nest to any depth. A flag supplied outside its elected scope is a distinct parse error naming the flag, its owning choice and the choice that was elected -- never "unknown flag". `strictcli.provided(record, "subject")` answers provided-ness inside a record; an env var or config key bound to a flag in a non-elected scope is not consulted and is named under `--verbose`; and the MCP projection flattens the scope into top-level properties (never in `required`) while publishing the scope structure in the tool description and refusing wrong combinations at call time with the CLI parser's own sentence.

**`MutexGroup` is removed.** Exactly-one-of-these is now a member-spelled choice flag, which carries the same rule with the type information kept rather than thrown away, adds a scope per member, and reproduces the mutex error sentences byte-for-byte. There is no shim and no deprecation period: replace `mutex=[MutexGroup(flags=[...])]` with `@strictcli.choice_flag(..., elect_by="member-flags", choices=[...])`, one `@strictcli.choice` class per member. A member flag now declares requiredness (read as *required once this member is elected*), inverting the old rule that forbade it.

**A `choices=` entry is always a record.** The bare-value entry is deleted: write `choices=[strictcli.Choice("head", help="push only the current HEAD branch"), strictcli.Choice("tags")]` instead of `choices=["head", "tags"]`, on flags and on positional args alike. Help on an entry is optional, and a flag whose entries carry help renders as an indented block instead of the one-line `[choices: a, b]` form. A bare entry is refused at registration with the record spelling in the message.

**A positional arg with helped choices renders an indented block.** The block rule was always content-keyed -- any `choices=` entry carrying help -- and it now reaches positional args exactly as it reaches flags: the entries render beneath the arg's line with their help, the one-line `[choices: a, b]` part is dropped in that form, and one alignment column is computed across the whole `Arguments:` section, deepest entry included.

**A structural parse problem is now reported ahead of a value that will not parse.** An unknown flag, an unknown choice and a scope violation are facts about the command line's shape, and shape is decided before any token's text is interpreted -- on every command, not only on one that declares a choice flag. `myapp cmd --count abc --unknown` reported `--count: expected integer, got 'abc'` and now reports `unknown flag '--unknown'`, and the answer no longer depends on which token came first.

**An integer `choices=` entry beyond ±2^53 is refused at registration.** The dumped schema publishes a declaration's choices as a JSON Schema `enum`, and a reader that parses JSON numbers as IEEE-754 doubles -- which every reader of a schema file is entitled to be -- reads a different integer back. Declare a big identifier as a string instead. Float choices are unaffected: the canonical float form round-trips exactly, so nothing is lost there.

**The MCP tool schema describes array parameters correctly.** A parameter whose value is a list carried its `enum` at the property root, which said the array itself had to equal one of the choices; it now sits inside `items`, describing an element. Two shapes were also projected as scalars and are now arrays: a repeatable flag and a variadic positional arg. All three follow from one arity rule, which the dumped `value_schema` fragment states as well, so a tool schema and a dumped schema cannot disagree about a value's shape.

**`--dump-schema` writes schema version 2.** A flag or arg entry carries a real JSON Schema fragment under `value_schema`, from a closed subset of `type`, `items`, `additionalProperties` and `enum` with JSON Schema's own type names; the `type` key and the `repeatable` key are gone, because arity is a property of the value and a repeatable flag publishes the same array fragment a `list[T]` flag does. A value flag's `choices=` splits in two: the values as an `enum` inside the fragment, and the value-plus-help records beside it under `choices` (`help` omitted when an entry declares none). A choice flag has no fragment at all -- its value is a variant the subset cannot express -- and instead publishes its nested choices and scopes, each scoped entry a full flag entry, with `elect_by` as the discriminator; choice flags now sit in the command's one `flags` array in declaration order rather than a separate key. Every entity's keys are emitted in a declared order, the document is written in one canonical encoding (canonical floats, raw UTF-8, no HTML escaping, two-space indent, one trailing newline) so two implementations' dumps are byte-comparable, and the `defaults` block is rewritten as the complete map of what an omitted key means. The dump also stops being blind to behavior: `config_format`, `config_path`, `config_conflict_mode`, per-flag `prefixed` and per-command `flag_sets` each appear exactly when a declaration departs from the framework's own behavior, `config_path` publishes the declaration rather than the machine's resolution of it, and the `checks` block is a function of the declaration alone rather than of whether a check has run in this process.

**A member's payload key elects its member at the machine boundary.** In the flat form the MCP and programmatic surfaces take, a payload key belonging to a member the selector key did not name was silently discarded: `{target: "all-profiles", profile: "work"}` ran with `all-profiles` elected and the profile name thrown away. Supplying a member's payload key is now electing that member, so that pair is refused as the double election it is, with the parser's own sentence (`--profile and --all-profiles are mutually exclusive`), and a payload key sent alone elects its member exactly as `--profile work` does on the command line.

**The README documents the schema-v2 dump and the scoped declaration surface.** The schema-dump section now states `schema_version: 2`, the `value_schema` fragment on every flag and arg entry, the choice flag's fragment-less `choices` plus `elect_by` encoding, and the canonical encoding that makes the three implementations' dumps byte-identical. The API tables gain `sub_flag`, `sub_choice_flag`, `member_value` and `provided`.

**The flat machine boundary reads a member key as the token it spells.** Two states of the flat form the MCP and programmatic surfaces take were answered wrongly. A key under a payload-less member's own name was ignored entirely, so `{all_profiles: true}` was refused with `one of --profile, --all-profiles is required` where `--all-profiles` elects on the command line; it now elects on `true` and declines on `false` exactly as `--no-all-profiles` does, decline clause included. And naming a payload-carrying member under the selector's own key without supplying that member's value -- `{mode: "profile"}` -- handed the command a record whose `str`-annotated, required field held `None`; it is now refused with the sentence the same mistake gets when typed, `flag '--profile' requires a value`. Both ride the ordinary tool-result error channel over MCP.

**A scoped flag's `RelativeToRoot` default reaches the handler as a path.** Declared inside a choice's scope, the marker was delivered as the `RelativeToRoot` object itself with source `default`, where the same declaration on a command-level flag delivers the resolved path with source `infra`. It now resolves through the declared infrastructure root at every depth, on the command line and at the machine boundary alike, and a marker naming an undeclared root is refused with the scope it was declared in.

**An unsatisfied member-spelled selector names the ambient election that caused it.** `one of --profile, --all-profiles is required under '--via email'` left out the clause naming the environment variable that elected the scope the requirement lives in, so the refusal blamed a command line that did not contain the cause. The three clauses now compose in one order -- scope, then origin, then the decline note -- with both parentheticals following a complete sentence.
